Letter from the Publisher

Starry-Eyed Optimism

The future is already here, and it’s not as frightening as it may seem.

The band Wilco has a lyric I think about almost daily: “Come on, children, you’re acting like children. Every generation thinks it’s the end of the world,” Jeff Tweedy croons in “You Never Know.” I’ve come to believe there’s a lot of wisdom packed into that line.

Read More

Lately, it can feel as though every conversation about the future of wine, or life in general, comes wrapped in a sense of impending doom. Whether it’s artificial intelligence, climate change, shifting consumer habits, politics, or economic uncertainty, it’s easy to mistake change for decline. But you won’t find much of that apocalyptic energy in these pages.

This issue is, in many ways, an antidote. Across nearly every profile in the Rising Stars feature, I was struck by the same themes: hospitality, curiosity, and connection. The talented people you’ll meet here aren’t ignoring change; they’re embracing it. They’re finding new ways to build community, preserve authenticity, and invite more people into the world of wine.

Innovation has never been the enemy of tradition. In wine, the two have always evolved together. Every generation inherits remarkable traditions, and every generation is responsible for finding new ways to keep them alive.

That’s exactly what this year’s Rising Stars are doing. They’re proving that what makes wine special isn’t changing. The ways we discover it, share it, and experience it are. And that’s something worth celebrating—no hand- wringing needed.

Each generation is confronted with its own version of a crisis. The successful ones look at it through the lens of possibility.

I hope these stories inspire you to do the same.

Rising Stars 2026

A celebration of emerging talent in the wine and spirits industry.

BY THE EDITORS OF WINE ENTHUSIAST

It’s hard to succeed in wine. Even if you inherited a vineyard, it takes patience and perseverance in the face of unfavorable economic and environmental forces. You need to possess a near-delusional sort of optimism to stay in the game when things go wrong. Then there are wildfires, mudslides, the rising cost of materials, and shifting drinking habits—it’s enough to make you hang it up and apply to law school.

But the industry isn’t only made up of winemakers. Sommeliers, importers, events producers, store owners, and media personalities each play a vital role in the global wine ecosystem. They’re often the ones on the frontlines, talking to people in restaurants and bars and on their screens, educating drinkers, hyping up unsung regions, and bringing new fans into the fold. 

Every year, we celebrate a new class of emerging talent in the drinks space. We solicit nominations from our editorial staff, writers-at-large, and former honorees, and then narrow the list down based on who has had the most impact. This year’s Rising Stars are a brilliant, international group of wine and spirits pros whose innovation and hard work is making the whole industry shine brighter. 

Ryan and Christopher Goydos

Co-Founders, SuperVinoBros
East Brunswick, NJ

“When we first got into wine, we had no idea that Beaujolais is primarily Gamay, that Sancerre is Sauvignon Blanc, or that red Burgundy means Pinot Noir. Those kinds of things seem obvious once you’ve spent time around wine, but they can feel completely confusing to someone just starting out. We think the industry sometimes forgets how overwhelming that learning curve can be.” 

Twin brothers Ryan and Christopher Goydos, a.k.a. SuperVinoBros, are a part of a new wave of wine media stars kicking dust off a category that often takes itself too seriously. They didn’t wait to get a certification to make videos about wine. They came in sideways during the pandemic, without the usual credentials, and their blind tastings quickly went viral on TikTok and Instagram.

SuperVinoBros started as a hobby and is now a multifaceted wine brand that spans videos, tours, tastings, and a wine club, all while keeping its messaging accessible and stripped of pretense. They translate wine terms without flattening them and explain grape varieties and regions clearly without losing the nuance that makes wine worth caring about. 

“The people doing the best work in wine right now are often the ones making it feel more welcoming, conversational, and connected to culture and everyday life,” Ryan says.

Scroll through their Instagram feed, and you’ll find them in Champagne drinking with producers, at a wine fair in Austria, or explaining German Pinot Noir to someone who doesn’t know much about wine.

Their audience reflects a shift that the industry is still trying to catch up with. Younger drinkers are stepping back from volume and leaning into meaning, gravitating toward organic, biodynamic, and natural wines, and asking who made them and why. The Goydos brothers meet that curiosity head-on, while pushing back against the fetishization culture that turns wine into something to protect rather than open.

What sets SuperVinoBros apart is the community they’ve built. It’s a welcoming space where no one has to perform expertise to belong. 

—Aleks Zecevic

Anthony Zraly

Chief Growth Officer,
T. Edward Wines & Spirits
New York, NY

“I find it shortsighted when restaurants or retailers define themselves through rigid absolutism—whether that means only natural wine or only grower Champagne, for example. Why are we creating increasingly divisive lines in an industry already facing significant challenges?”

Anthony Zraly has always had a nose for wine. Born into a family of wine pros, some of his earliest memories involve exploring the cellars of López de Heredia in Rioja before he started kindergarten. He may or may not have been popping corks professionally before he could drive a car.

But it’s not the past that excites Anthony. It’s the future, which he believes is far more promising than many jaded industry veterans care to admit. “Some of the most innovative people today are finding ways to preserve wine’s depth and culture while making it feel more emotionally accessible and culturally relevant to younger audiences,” he says.

This sentiment lies at the core of everything Anthony is trying to achieve at importer T. Edward. “I view my role as bridging tradition and innovation in an industry that is evolving quickly and being challenged to rethink many long-standing assumptions,” he tells us.

He’s always pushing to make wine more vibrant and alive, with a focus on spreading enjoyment and knowledge without the accompanying dogma: “Wine should inspire discovery, pleasure, hospitality, and conversation, not ideological tribalism.”

In Zraly’s view, pronounced tribalism is a huge part of today’s communication problem. Old World vs. New World. Natty vs. traditional. These battle lines aren’t helping anyone, he says. “Some of the most exciting conversations happen in the gray areas rather than the extremes.”

—Tom R. Capo

Alex Sarovich

Founder & CEO,
Own Rooted Hospitality
Sonoma County, CA

“We have the most engaged wine-drinking generation we’ve ever seen, and a distribution infrastructure that makes it genuinely difficult for the best small producers to reach them. That’s the thing I’d fix tomorrow.”

After an early career with elite restaurants like SingleThread Farms in Sonoma and Attica in Melbourne, Alex Sarovich could have done what many successful sommeliers do, and taken a cushy job with a big wine company. These sorts of roles are prime opportunities for wine pros ready to stop working the floor at night.

But not Sarovich. She looked at the modern wine landscape, and considered the plight of producers she’d gotten to know over her years in restaurants. She saw the gap between successful winemaking and meaningful connection to the industry, especially across the hard-to-navigate three-tier system. That’s when her agency, Own Rooted Hospitality, was born.

Sarovich sees her raison d’être as “Connecting people to the wines and the humans behind them that deserve to be known. Creating experiences where something real happens between people.” She spends her days leveraging her connections across the industry to raise visibility for small brands in and around her home in Sonoma County. This might mean managing PR, developing events, or building brand visibility in today’s increasingly complex wine market.

For Sarovich, the future of wine centers around the next generation of consumers, with a focus on greater equity and access for everyone who wants a place at the table. “Wine has historically been an intimidating and exclusionary world,” she says, “and I want to be part of changing that.”

—Tom R. Capo

Michael Aredes

Founder/Bartender,
Noche Traviesa New York, NY

“A trip to Denny’s with family prompted my love for being in hospitality in general—seeing how happy everyone was when the team was making people feel good through their service.”

Michael Aredes is the founder and self-proclaimed head troublemaker of Noche Traviesa, a pop-up event series that features queer Latinx bartenders, performers, venues, and brand sponsors. He’s on a mission to create a safe, fun, and wild space for people to get into what he calls “that good trouble.” In his own words, he is “great at throwing stupid fun parties with dumb good drinks and immaculate vibes.”

Noche Traviesa events highlight participants through cocktails and performances and create a lively, supportive space for guests to come together and enjoy their lives. The parties multiply joy in a world where we forget to experience it regularly, he says.

Prior to launching Noche Traviesa, Aredes was part of the opening team at Superbueno, an acclaimed NYC bar that ranked No. 2 on the North America’s 50 Best Bars list. But the idea for Noche Traviesa dates back even further. After feeling unwelcome and experiencing downright hostility in some venues, Aredes wanted to create a welcoming space for anyone who had ever felt the same way.

By the spring of 2024, Noche Traviesa was born. Since then, Aredes has hosted over 30 pop-up events in the U.S. and Puerto Rico, and he is proud of everything that has blossomed from the simple foundation of building community around joy.

“By creating more diverse spaces and opinions,” he says, “we allow ourselves to learn more, to disrupt systems that no longer serve us, and to ignite fire in younger generations to keep going forward—maintaining our industry and letting it evolve.”

—Maeve Wade

Giacomo Bartolommei

President, Consorzio del Vino Brunello di Montalcino and Winemaker,
Caprili Montalcino, Italy

“We talk about today’s wine industry as if it were uniquely in crisis—tariffs, declining consumption, climate, regulation—and we forget our own history.”

Giacomo Bartolommei, 34, has been drawing attention for his youth, but his vision is one of longevity. Elected to be the president of the Consorzio del Vino Brunello di Montalcino in 2025, he’s a native of the region and a winemaker himself, working the vineyard his grandfather planted in 1965 at his family estate, Caprilli.

Bartolommei is leading Montalcino from personal experience as much as from expertise, and his investment in the region is personal as well as professional. As the industry faces challenges, he’s not worried for the future, nor is he stuck in the past—he’s interested in capturing the magical energy that comes from the tension between the two.

After studying economics in college, he returned home for the 2016 harvest. “There is something almost vertiginous about making a wine in 2016 that someone will uncork in 2046 at a birthday or a wedding that I’ll never see,” he says. “That is the work. That is what lights me up every morning and what I now carry into the consorzio as well.” In the intervening moment, here in 2026, Bartolommei is already shining in his new role.

If he could snap his fingers and change one thing in the wine world tomorrow? “I would give producers the courage to go back to thinking in decades, not quarters.” He would remind the industry that the “greatest chapters of wine history have always been written by people who refused to be intimidated by the crisis of their moment.”

—Danielle Callegari

Claudia Castro

Postdoctoral Scientist,
U.S. Department of Agriculture
El Cerrito, CA

“As a scientist, you’ll never know the answer to everything. It’s what makes it fun and keeps you humble.”

Where there’s wildfire smoke, you’ll find molecular biologist Claudia Castro hard at work. Castro works for the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Agricultural Research Service, where she pursues “the discovery of grape-associated bacteria that consume smoke-taint-causing volatile phenols and the enzymes involved in this process.” In other words, she’s fighting the good fight against smoke taint.

Her pursuits have already yielded promising results. Research conducted by Castro and her colleagues was recently published in the scientific journal PLOS One. The group discovered that Gordonia alkanivorans, a bacteria that lives on grapevines, can degrade guaiacol, a volatile phenol found in woodsmoke.

Guaiacol released during wildfires can damage grapes and cause ashy qualities in wine. Although they are still in the early stages of research, Castro and her team hope that taking a microbial approach to removing unwanted volatile phenols from grapes and must will one day help minimize wildfire damage. This is good news for everyone, since smoke taint costs wineries millions of dollars each year.

It’s a labor of love for Castro, who credits growing up surrounded by farmland in northwest Mexico as one of her primary inspirations for working with grapes. “I’m proud to come from a multigenerational lineage of farmers,” she says. Her passion was also ignited by “the elegance of plant physiology and the significant cultural, economic, and human health impact of grapes.”

—Michael Alberty

Ren Peir

Sommelier and Queer Community Organizer
Brooklyn, NY

“A moment I still get emotional about is when one of my somms said to me that they’d never felt like their full self at work, and BABE was the first time they felt free and fully embodied.”

Ren Peir walked away from a 15-year tech career with one clear intention: to use wine as a tool to reclaim space for queer folks of color. She co-founded the monthly pop-up, BABE Wine Bar, which would take over a space and operate as an RSVP-only bar, fully staffed by a team of queer sommeliers of color.

Peir’s role spanned everything from brand building, design, and partnerships, to accounting, wine buying, and floor service. What made her work so powerful is that, operationally, BABE was a beautifully executed hospitality concept. Philosophically, it was a reclamation of who gets to be a wine person. “To walk into a space built for you feels like you’ve been running in oxygen-thin air,” Peir says. “And finally you can fill your lungs with the richness of safety, community, and joy.”

The results spoke for themselves: “When I initially was seeking mentorship to open a ‘wine bar only for queer folks,’ I mostly received skepticism and discouragement,” she says. “After two years of running BABE, I not only saw a packed house month after month, but also more and more affinity-centered wine concepts or wine in alternative spaces.”

The feedback from guests was glowing, like the one who told her, “I never thought I was allowed to be a wine girlie. But now I know, I AM a wine girlie.” Peir is currently in the process of opening a queer wine bar with its own permanent space.

—Anna-Christina Cabrales

Milena Berman

Co-Founder, Hautes Côtes, Vin et Hip Hop, and TERRA
Beaune, France

“Viticulture has found its space in what I consider ‘the cultural sphere.’ Winemakers are creators, and culture is about cultivation, whether it’s ideas, cultural products, or, in this case, vines.”

Originally from San Francisco, Milena Berman moved to Burgundy in 2013 to work for a travel company that organized museum tours. She thought she’d stay in France for a few years—until she landed a job at Domaine Dujac and shifted her focus to wine.

Over a decade later, the Beaune-based cultural producer has made a name for herself by building bridges between wine and a wide array of creative industries, spanning art, design, music, and fashion. In addition to organizing wine and art trips for Hautes Côtes with her partner, Loïc Lamy, Berman produces popular events like Vin et Hip Hop, a tasting party co-created with Jeremy Seysses of Domaine Dujac, and TERRA, an art exhibition across cultural heritage sites, co-founded with curator Jenn Ellis.

Her goal? To open doors and make connections to bring the wine and art worlds closer together. “The art world can be intimidated by wine and vice versa,” she says. “What both sides are lacking is access, education, and openness by the other side to receive them.”

Berman has been impressed by the growing number of wineries reaching out to new audiences, as well as the community that has grown around her cross-cultural gatherings. “There is an infectious element in the parties, exhibitions, tastings, and concerts,” she says. “It is the people—our team, who work so hard to prepare them, and the guests—who give them life.”

—Sara Ventiera

Kilolo Strobert

Owner & Operator,
Fermented Grapes Wines & Spirits
Brooklyn, NY

“Everyone should have a dream. If you don’t have one, start thinking about something wild you want to achieve.”

Brooklyn-born and -raised Kilolo Strobert took a giant leap when she took the reins of the longstanding Prospect Heights bottle shop Fermented Grapes Wine & Spirits at the height of the pandemic in 2021.

But after working in the wine industry for 17 years—including as the first full-time employee of Fermented Grapes, which she followed with stints at Zagat and FreshDirect—she was precisely the right woman for the job. “My work as a wine professional is rooted in hospitality,” says Strobert, who also serves as the communications coordinator for the nonprofit Wine on Wheels, which raises funds to empower people with disabilities. “That means that my passion is rooted in making sure that people feel taken care of.”

Whether she’s posting about her favorite Txakolinas on Instagram or advising customers on the best wine pairings for a spicy chicken sandwich from Wendy’s, Strobert has an unwavering belief in the power of wine to build community when it is accessible to all. At a time when the industry is rethinking how it sells wine, her work proves that the neighborhood shop remains fundamental to a healthy—and vibrant—wine ecosystem.

“I believe in listening to one’s soul and humans respecting one another,” she says. “My passion for wine ignited when I understood that I could facilitate happiness through helping please customers’ palates.”

—Maria Yagoda

Jeanne Feldkamp
and Dan Diephouse

Founders, Co-Owners, and Co-Winemakers,
Corollary Wines Amity, OR

“Neither of us worked in wine before starting Corollary. Jeanne designed red-carpet dresses, did marketing for tech startups, and still runs an interior design studio. Dan worked in product and engineering in tech. But weirdly, running the winery brings together all the threads of our lives. We love the act of creation, designing, and building something.”

Jeanne Feldkamp and Dan Diephouse are “all in” on Oregon sparkling wine, which is the only thing they make at Corollary Wines. This is only their 10th harvest, but given their impact, it feels like they’ve been making bubbles in the Willamette Valley for decades.

Building on their commitment, Feldkamp and Diephouse recently gained attention as founding board members of Method Oregon, a nonprofit consortium of 55 producers dedicated to sharing the story of traditional method sparkling wine from the state.

Members of Method Oregon adhere to established guidelines regarding fruit origins, farming, production, and labeling to earn the “Method Oregon” mark on their bottles. By 2029, qualifying labels must also specify the American Viticultural Area(s) of origin and a disgorgement date.

Feldkamp and Diephouse hope their efforts with Method Oregon will “bring Oregon traditional method sparkling wines to the world stage.”

Their journey to making outstanding sparkling wines began after careers in design and technology, respectively. Reflecting on this transition, is there anything they wish people had told them back then? “Yes,” Feldkamp says. “That 80% of owning a winery is marketing; the other 20% is cleaning barrels and tanks. We’re only slightly kidding; we still love it.”

—Michael Alberty

Peter Andrews

Founder & President, Culture Wine Co. and Co-Founder, Hella Chenin Wine Fest
San Francisco, CA

“The wine industry has a habit of talking itself into crisis, and it’s not a great look. Create a compelling product, know your customer, stay disciplined, and people will come. Nobody wants to be part of something that feels desperate.”

South Africa is producing some of the world’s most exciting wine, but the category remains woefully underrepresented in the U.S. California-based importer Peter Andrews is on a mission to change that.

In 2022, burned out on the industry, he took a trip to South Africa that reignited his joy for wine and changed his life. “I came home, wrote a business plan, and returned just a couple of months later,” he says. “I drove over 1,000 kilometers, met with 50 winemakers, and signed nine producers on that trip alone.”

Andrews’ Culture Wine Co. is an importer, wholesaler, and e-commerce retailer focused exclusively on South African wine. He’s made some big bets over the past few years, and they’ve been paying off with placements at Michelin-starred tasting menus, top wine bars, and leading independent bottle shops. He’s not just building his own business; he’s cultivating enthusiasm for an entire country.

A key part of his master plan is Hella Chenin, a wine festival and pop-up series devoted entirely to Chenin Blanc. The first two festivals have been a smashing success, drawing big Millennial and Gen Z crowds to Hammerling Wines in Berkeley. “Young people aren’t walking away from wine,” he says. “They’re waiting for the industry to meet them where they are.”

A South African wine importer trying to make Chenin Blanc cool? We see what you’re doing there, and we like it.

—Ryan Grim

Cokie Ponikvar

Creative Director,
Cokie’s World of Wine
London, New York, and Toronto

“Fostering my excitement and protecting it from people who don’t quite understand it yet has been critical.”

Cokie Ponikvar began her wine journey the way so many others have—by watching the 2012 documentary Somm. But unlike many people inspired by the film, Ponikvar, at just 25 years old, is already a Master of Wine and Master Sommelier candidate.

Lucky for us, she doesn’t keep her oenological studies to herself. What began as a way for her parents and friends to follow her wine education on Instagram has evolved into Cokie’s World of Wine, a brand with nearly half a million followers.

Ponikvar’s content is mostly comprised of her blind tastings and exam prep, plus videos exploring every corner of the wine world, like how corks are made, food pairings, and nitty-gritty scientific details. “There is an incredible opportunity to add value through wine knowledge,” she says. “Getting people excited about wine is like creating free happiness out of thin air.”

For Ponikvar, wine has always been more about the pursuit of knowledge than drinking. Over the past few years, she’s stepped into the role of educator, becoming one of wine’s most compelling new voices by making the topic feel welcoming instead of intimidating. In doing so, she’s inspired a new generation of wine lovers to explore what’s in the glass—and everything that comes with it.

—Jordon Kaplan

Jess Druey 

Founder, Whiny Wines
Santa Rosa, CA

“When I entered wine, I was honestly intimidated. I had no connections, no family background in the industry, and I was often the youngest person in the room. But I also entered at a moment where the industry seemed more willing to listen and evolve.”

Jess Druey stumbled into launching a wine revolution by accident. She was trying to buy a bottle of wine for a date and wound up feeling completely overwhelmed.

“I realized wine itself wasn’t the problem—the way it was being presented was,” says the Bakersfield, California, native. “That moment sparked my mission to help make wine feel more approachable, emotionally relevant, and culturally connected for younger consumers.”

She launched Whiny Baby in 2022, targeting Gen Z consumers with three original wines—red, white, and fizzy pink—whose bottles featured easy-to-pop caps, conversation prompts, peel-off labels for saving memories, and even beaded charms. She was 24 years old, with no industry connections. Whiny Baby grew into a nationally recognized brand focused on introducing the next generation to wine through curiosity, storytelling, and approachable California blends.

After selling the brand to Gallo in 2025, Druey remains in charge of the renamed Whiny Wines while consulting on consumer innovation within the larger company. She’s also at work on a book tentatively called Whine With Me: A Field Guide to American Wine, to be published in 2027.

“I’m most proud of the real human connections this work has brought into my life,” she says. “Wine, at its best, is about people—conversation, gathering, memory, laughter, vulnerability, celebration—and I’m proud that the products and experiences I’ve created have been able to enhance those moments for others.”

—Matt Kettmann

title: This Bitter, Earthy Cocktail Is Just Right for Sweater Weather
summary:
Equal parts Cynar, Aperol, bourbon, and lemon juice, the Unknown Vegetable is full of earthy, vegetal depth.

The post This Bitter, Earthy Cocktail Is Just Right for Sweater Weather appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
No other author plays with the gothic motifs of Halloween quite like Edward Gorey. His illustrated books are moody and macabre, but also whimsical and darkly funny. The Gashlycrumb Tinies (1963) is his famed alphabet book, in which each letter introduces a child who meets a grim yet oddly hilarious fate. (“A is for Amy, who fell down the stairs; B is for Basil, assaulted by bears.”)

The Unknown Vegetable is a nuanced, bittersweet cocktail that pays homage to Gorey’s story of the same name, in which a woman hears a sound “that came from underneath the ground.” She watches a stalk grow, then wrenches it from the earth, takes it home, and eats it. As you can imagine, her encounter with the unknown vegetable does not end well.

In this drink, the “unknown vegetable” refers to artichoke, the dominant flavoring in Cynar, an Italian amaro. The original template for the cocktail, the Paper Plane, was created at NYC’s Milk & Honey (now Attaboy) by Sam Ross in 2008. This twist swaps out sweeter, milder Amaro Nonino Quintessentia for Cynar, which adds vegetal, earthy, bitter depth.

The end result is a slow-sipping quaff with an inscrutable ’choke note—a haunting combination Gorey likely would have approved.

title: Where to Drink Wine in Mexico City
summary:
Amid booming tourism, CDMX’s wine scene is coming into its own, with wine bars and bottle shops flourishing across the capital.

The post Where to Drink Wine in Mexico City appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
For a country known for its gastronomic pleasures, Mexico drinks surprisingly little wine—roughly six glasses per person each year, about one-tenth the average in the United States. And yet one of the most dynamic and fast- growing wine scenes in the Americas can be found in Mexico City (CDMX). As its reputation as a global food destination has grown and tourism has surged, the city has seen a remarkable wave of wine bars and wine-focused restaurants.

Not even 10 years ago, the options were slim. Halfway decent wine lists were mostly confined to fine-dining restaurants and a handful of corporate-style wine bars pouring mass-market labels, while many neighborhood bars skipped wine altogether or offered a lonely bottle of forgettable supermarket red. Then, around the start of the pandemic, several trends converged: interest in natural wine—both Mexican and imported—accelerated, U.S. visitors started coming in droves due to low prices and no pandemic restrictions, hospitality businesses embraced more informal bar-centric formats, and a new flock of entrepreneurs launched wine clubs, delivery services, and importing projects.

“The explosion of natural wine about six years ago was really the first step,” says Antonio Nates of Tierras de Uva. “From there it either sparked or coincided with a broader push for learning and discovery. Mexican consumers started moving away from big, status-driven reds toward whites, skin- contact wines, and a greater sense of curiosity.”

The momentum didn’t stop there. Wine education in the city expanded through classes, tastings, and festivals, while sommeliers such as Laura Santander and Sandra Fernández gained visibility alongside some of the country’s best-known chefs. Bottle shops like Vinos Chidos and Escorpio evolved into community gathering spaces with regular events.

Recently, a few restaurants have opened adjacent wine bars to keep the party rolling, like Meroma’s bar Vecino, Taller de Ostiones by FISM’s Baby Bar, and Fantasma, a bottle shop and wine bar attached to the wine-driven restaurant Fugaz. Mexico City is even home to what may be North America’s only Chinese natural wine and dumpling shop, Vía Sol, where owner Iris Yu imports tiny-production wines from China and serves them alongside like-minded bottles from around the world.

Today, Mexico City has no shortage of places to drink wine, and these standouts offer more than impressive lists. They combine thoughtful curation, knowledgeable staff, proper storage and serving temperatures, quality stemware, and genuinely welcoming hospitality that continues to change the city’s drinking culture for the better.

Brutal Vinata de Barrio

IG @brutalvinatadebarrio

Opened in 2022 by Alex Langlois and Francisca Riffo, Brutal Vinata de Barrio is a proper cave à manger in the leafy San Miguel Chapultepec neighborhood just west of Condesa. Equal parts bottle shop and wine bar, most guests stop in for a couple of glasses from the extensive, ever-changing by-the-glass list, which ranges from Australia to Austria and is priced close to retail (the only requirement is that the wines are “small producers making wines with soul”). Yet the food is an underrated draw, and those in the know cobble together long lunches of dishes like burrata in green-apple gazpacho and oxtail sandwich with black garlic and pickles, paired with bottles bought off the shelf with nominal corkage fees. They also own Chabela Bocaderia & Ultramarinos in the same neighborhood, a kind of ultramodern tapas bar (albeit one with a bacon-and-Emmental Wagyu burger), with several vermouths and Sherries by the glass.

The owners cite the joy of seeing locals so eager to learn about wine, despite—or perhaps because of—the lack of an omnipresent wine culture. “Mexicans, of course, have great taste,” says the French-born Langlois. “They may not think they have the words to talk about wine, but they definitely have the palate.”

Hugo

IG @hugoelwinebar

Hugo is a wine bar that seems imported from Brooklyn except for gentler pricing and outdoor tables set among giant agave and Art Deco architecture. While Hugo’s menu, from Chef Michael Crespo, is mostly veg- and seafood-driven small plates, its neighbor, Bar Nino, is a full-service restaurant where the food and wine use Italy as a launchpad and then go in myriad directions.

“The community around wine here is great—young people who are scrappy and well educated about wine, food, and service,” says wine director Gus Gasson, who runs both programs with sommelier Sofía Sánchez. He says the influence of importers can’t be overstated, noting that availability has grown exponentially over the last two years. “There’s an attitude of ‘I have to import this if I want to drink it’ and a ton of upstarts who have both the knowledge and the motivation.”

Natas

IG @nataswines

Blink, and you’ll miss Natas, a tiny, stylish wine bar that nonetheless offers 100-plus wines at retail, several by the glass, and an impressive menu from a barely existent kitchen that might include Vietnamese spring rolls or a tuna melt with Sicilian caponata. One wall is mostly French wines (owner David Nicholson is originally from France); the other mostly Mexican. All share a philosophy of native yeast, minimal added sulfur, and small personal projects with character. Frequent guests and pop-ups make it feel as much like an event space as a buzzy bar.

Lenez

IG @lenez_mx

Lenez owner Wilton Romero Nava was wine director at Quintonil (one of the country’s most acclaimed restaurants), and later an importer and distributor of premium German wine before opening Lenez in 2025. It quickly earned a reputation for its deep wine selection, knowledgeable staff, and thoughtful approach. There are always at least 16 glass pours (all available by half glass for half the price), from Thierry Germain’s “L’Insolite” Chenin to a 2016 Cascina Baricchi Barbaresco. Yet the bottle list rivals that of any restaurant in town, with back vintages and allocated wines; ask for a cellar tour to get ideas. As its popularity has grown, so has the kitchen, with the menu changing as often as the glass list: tapas-inspired bites, market-inspired salads, and elaborate housemade pastas.

NIV

IG @nivbar.mx

The importer and distributor Les Climats has over 10 years of experience delivering premium, mostly European wine to the city’s best restaurants. When owner Tanguy de Bodinat opened NIV in 2023, it was a way to get these wines (and others he loves but doesn’t represent) into more hands. A short menu from Chef Diego Martínez skews equally French bistro (steak frites) and Italian (tomato tonnato, “Máster Raviolo” of egg yolk and ricotta), with bar snacks like anchovy toast and green-olive baba ghanoush. It also has precise cocktails, pét-nats, orange wines, and turntables, but never feels trendy or pretentious due to de Bodinat’s obsession with quality and timelessness. The indoor tables are romantic, but standing is welcome during busy times, and the street scene is always good for people-watching.

Wine Country,
Led by Wine Enthusiast

Oropel

IG @oropelcdmx

It’s hard to find a wine lover in CDMX who doesn’t have a soft spot for Oropel, one of the hippest wine bars in town. A huge vermouth selection, natural wines like Barrigón Xarel-lo/Macabeo from a few hours north in Querétaro, and classic Negronis are piled on rickety outdoor tables that feel more like a street party than a demure wine tasting. There are weekly guest chefs, winemakers, and spirits producers, plus collabs with other restaurants and bars, all amplifying the conviviality of the city’s wine and bar scene. If you’re both kind and lucky, you might be treated to the mythical late-night chicken shot, but— like the allocated wines that frequently find their way into Oropel— it’s something you have to be offered, and can’t be ordered.

Plonk

IG @plonk.mx

Plonk is the project of two of Mexico City’s most respected wine and restaurant figures: Sommelier Romina Argüelles, named Michelin’s Top Sommelier in Mexico in 2025, and Chef Flor Camorlinga, whose Asian-inflected cooking has earned a national following. Her menu might feature dishes such as miso-glazed bone marrow with squash blossoms or grilled fish finished with a seaweed-jalapeño sauce. The wine list runs to around 100 bottles, mostly from Europe, with a clear focus on sustainable farming, low-intervention winemaking, and wines that reflect their place of origin. The location doesn’t hurt either, with terrace seating on quiet Calle Iztaccíhuatl, just steps from Parque México in the heart of Condesa.

Si Mon

IG @vinos_simon

While Mexican wine is growing in popularity in the U.S., it’s still rare to find more than a few bottles in Mexico City bars and restaurants, partly due to an oppressive tax structure for artisanal wine and beer that dissuades exploration. Nevertheless, Si Mon has the biggest selection in town, both as a bottle shop and in its glass selection, with a smart and comprehensive list of Mexican spirits and craft beers for your cross-drinking friends. Priority is given to smaller family producers, and the selection spans all of Mexico (not just the larger wine-producing regions of Valle de Guadalupe and Coahuila), and staff is eager to discuss the diversity of Mexican wine with anyone who will listen.

Tierras de Uva

IG @tierrasdeuva

Whatever you need Tierras de Uva to be, it delivers: a retail shop of less-seen Spanish and Portuguese wines; a market for Spanish cured meats, tinned fish, and other provisions; an importer showroom; a wine bar with several bottles open at any given time and a “Chill It” machine for insta-chilling any bottle off the shelf. As importers, Tierras de Uva’s owners work with over 70 producers, most from small regions or making innovative wines in established regions. Sommelier Antonio Nates says he’s seen tastes move from people asking for 100-point Ribera del Duero to wines from Sierras de Gredo in the Vinos de Madrid DO, unfortified “vinos de pasto” from Jerez and Montilla-Moriles, and a following for Antonio Maçanita’s wines made from less-known native Portuguese grapes.

“Storytelling is key,” says Nates. “People don’t just ask for ‘natural wine’ as much anymore, but they do want to know the stories behind who made the wine and how they made it. CDMX is the perfect place to do what we do because people are always looking for new things, in wine as well as food.”

Vigneron

IG @vigneronmx

Vigneron opened in 2020 as a sort of showroom for the French wines the owners imported, a Parisian-inspired jewel box of a wine bar with light snacks from rotating chefs. It’s evolved into a wine bar/restaurant hybrid with Michelin acclaim, and inspired many of the other spots on this list. For a place whose service model—from glassware to temperature to Coravin pours—is so meticulous, it’s surprisingly unpretentious: Staffers spark conversations about sparkling wine before dropping off printed menus, often bringing multiple bottles to taste. “It’s like music,” says sommelier Arturo Ramírez. “There are people who like commercial music and people who like esoteric music, but the fun is to turn people on to the music we love.”

title: How Have We Lived So Long Without Portuguese Bubbles?
summary:
Historically, Portugal is one of the last places you’d expect to find Champagne-style wines, but the country's sparkling landscape has been evolving.

The post How Have We Lived So Long Without Portuguese Bubbles? appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
It was a revelatory shock. Ages ago, on my first-ever trip to Porto, I stood in a bottle shop, dumbfounded by the abundance of Portuguese traditional-method sparkling wines on the shelves. Why is Portuguese bubbly not a thing elsewhere? I wondered.

Historically, Portugal is one of the last places you’d expect to find Champagne-style wines. The average drinker is completely oblivious to the country’s high-quality traditional-method bottlings—they are the Mr. Cellophane to Vinho Verde’s Roxie Hart, for the Chicago fans out there. But the Portuguese sparkling landscape has been evolving, with producers slowly making international inroads here and there. And in what can still be a stubbornly patriarchal industry, it’s notably women winemakers who have been bubbling to the top.

From France With Love… And a Side of Sardines

The Portuguese realize the sparkling world still revolves around those chalky hills billowing out from Reims and Épernay. They’re not here to reinvent the wheel or claim the crown. They’re just trying to give Champagne’s venerable heritage an inimitable Lusophone accent.

It all began by the ocean, in the weather-beaten basin of Bairrada. Local lore holds that Napoleon’s troops introduced Champagne-method production to the area during their ill-fated invasion of Portugal in the early 1800s. The Portuguese-British alliance drove the French out in 1811, but it wasn’t until the 1890s that Portuguese wineries began producing sparkling wine on a commercial scale. Now, with all things fizz in fashion, and with Portugal’s international profile continuing to surge, the country’s overlooked traditional-method wines may finally have a fighting chance to carve out serious space in markets abroad.

The Other, Other Vinho Verde

North of Bairrada, in the corner of the country known for “green wine,” a revolution of sorts has been underway.

“Vinho Verde is not the obstacle. The simplification of it abroad is,” lamented Maria João Cerdeira, co-owner at Soalheiro in the far northern reaches of the Minho region. The inexpensive, fizzy style known to supermarket coldboxes worldwide—not that there’s anything wrong with it—has left the region a victim of its own mass-market success. “Vinho Verde is a diverse region, with distinct subregions, noble grape varieties, and the capacity to produce serious wines, including traditional-method sparkling,” she insisted.

Her family’s estate, a household name for still wines since 1974, raised the bar for regional fizz with Iberia’s first traditional-method Alvarinho back in 1995. Originally a veterinarian by trade, Cerdeira returned to work at the family business several years ago, and now oversees the entire operation. In 2024, another woman, the gifted Asun Carballo, ascended to lead the winemaking team, forming a formidable duo that is now pushing the winery toward new heights.

“What first caught my interest was not the [Champagne method] itself, but the idea that Alvarinho—a variety so deeply identified with our region as a still wine—could express itself in a completely different language,” Cerdeira said.

Other local varieties, like Loureiro and Azal, are more easily tamed into a balanced sparkling. With Alvarinho, it’s a tightrope walk to capture its special aromatic flamboyance while holding onto restraint and finesse. “For sparkling, we return to the roots of the variety: lower alcohol, lower pH, higher natural acidity, and more linearity,” she explained. “[It’s] a base wine that holds back, allowing time on lees to shape its complexity.”

Vinho Verde and the Minho region are coming of age, shedding the reputational shackles of cheap-and-cheerful supermarket wine and a patriarchal mentality. “We are seeing a new generation of women in Portuguese wine taking on leading roles, bringing a complementary sensibility—attention to detail, long-term thinking, and care for both people and place,” she said. “It’s not a coincidence, but neither is it a movement defined by gender. It reflects how the industry itself is evolving.”

Mining Portugal’s Mountainous Core

Meanwhile, to the southeast, Marta Lourenço is ensuring that Portugal’s most beloved traditional-method winery remains an icon. Wedged high in the mountains between Douro and Dão is a small region called Távora-Varosa, and its most famous winery, Murganheira, produces what many Portuguese call their “Champagne brand.” Bringing a bottle of Murganheira Super Reserva Bruto—with its instantly recognizable tuxedo-black-and-gold label—makes a statement in the average Portuguese household.

Sure, it’s only about 15 euros at the local supermarket. But in a country where the average spend for a local bottle is between five and 10 euros, that’s a splurge. Every time I’ve brought it to a party, even the wealthier, hardcore wine snobs hold out their glasses.

For almost 20 years now, Murganheira and its sister operation, Raposeira, have been lucky enough to have Lourenço calling the shots.

In the cellars and caves of Távora-Varosa, she and her team craft the flagship classics of Portugal’s only DOC that’s almost exclusively dedicated to traditional-method bubbly.

But that wasn’t her original plan.

“My life’s dream was quite different—to be an occupational therapist,” admitted Lourenço. “Since I didn’t achieve that, life naturally led me down this path.” And as if on cue, France made an entrance. “I soon understood that I had to travel to Champagne,” she said. “To ‘take the leap,’ because of the technique and know-how for rigor and excellence.”

While Lourenço will always be influenced by her time in Champagne, she maintains that her mountain region is unlike anything else. “In Távora-Varosa, we achieve the natural freshness of Champagne, but because we have more hours of sunshine, our grapes have superior aromatic maturation, which translates into our sparkling wines,” she said. “We have [some] that we harvest with 13.5% [potential alcohol], and they still arrive with 17 grams of acidity. That’s what makes us so special.”

Ambassador of the Central Coast

It’s easy to feel bad for the vines of Portugal’s central coast. They take a brutal beating from the Atlantic. “They told me when coming to Portugal that there is sun,” complained a fellow passenger on a recent visit with Daniel Niepoort, rising star of the celebrated Niepoort winemaking clan. “This isn’t Portugal,” Daniel replied. “This is Bairrada.”

It was a statement of both complaint and adoration.

The limestone-clay soils and ocean-lashed climate produce wines of incredible tension, salinity, and complexity. If traditional-method bottlings from Vinho Verde are the exuberant, expressive upstarts—and those from the mountains of Távora-Varosa the noble classics—Bairrada bubbly is quickly becoming the gastronomic darling of sommeliers worldwide. It’s why the region’s winemakers ironically embrace their moody kingdom by the sea.

A few days later, I arrived for an audience with Filipa Pato, a legend of Bairrada. While once known primarily as the daughter of Luís Pato, the region’s winemaking godfather, she—along with husband-partner William Wouters—has arguably risen to even greater heights through her unrelenting curiosity and biodynamic methodologies.

Leveraging the inherent balance and harmony of the local flora and fauna teases out wines of ethereal delicacy and detail. “Before climate change, Bairrada was not an easy region for still wines,” she said. “In many years, ripening was difficult. You maybe had two or three really good vintages per decade. So making high-quality sparkling wine was not only a stylistic choice; it was almost a natural necessity.”

Carving out a niche in the shadow of her father was no easy road, though. For years, the chemical engineer-turned-vigneron toiled in bare-bones, garagiste fashion—patiently learning and listening to what the terroir had to say. “I started in 2001 from scratch. There was no money, no property, no help from anyone. Only my grandmother, who gave me the opportunity to start in my grandfather’s old winery,” she recalled. “There was almost nothing, just walls.”

At the time, Bairrada was still a footnote on the global stage. Producers plied their craft and built slowly. Joining forces professionally in 2006 with William, a renowned Belgian sommelier and restaurateur, boosted their international visibility, and they rebranded as Filipa Pato & William Wouters. But that didn’t mean the challenges of being a female winemaker vanished overnight. “It wasn’t so easy,” she said. “As a woman in Portugal, you had to insist more—and in many ways, that’s still true today.”

Playing the Long Game

Nothing here—aside from cars and rent prices— moves fast. Lunches demand hours of commitment, conversations are epic sagas, wine is drunk slowly (if copiously), and getting the check quickly is nearly impossible.

Anything else would be wholly un-Portuguese.

Fittingly, international appreciation for the country’s traditional-method bubbly is growing gradually, modestly, and in baby steps. Like a friendship with the locals, it’s taking its own sweet, stubborn, frustrating time. But once embraced, you’ll wonder how the hell you’ve ever gotten along without them.

Bottles to Look For

Filipa Pato NV 3B Brut Nature Rosé Sparkling (Bairrada)

Rich red berries and suave texture are grounded by racy acidity and subtle salinity in the estate’s brilliant entrylevel offering. Gastronomic and downright fun to drink.

$22 K&L Wine Merchants

Murganheira 2022 Super Reserva Bruto (Távora-Varosa)

Bringing classic scents of baked green apple, hazelnut, and brioche to go with a creamy texture and a centering core of citrus and mineral.

$18 Granvine

Soalheiro NV Alvarinho Bruto (Minho)

The peachy-floral glow of Alvarinho is tamed by crisp apple and tangerine-hued citrus, all anchored by a whisper of brioche and lick of wet stone.

$18 Portugal Vineyards

Quinta das Bágeiras 2022 Super Reserva Bruto Natural (Bairrada)

Serves up dried orchard fruit and floral aromas with a side of rising dough, oyster shell, and saline minerality. Classy and poised while irresistibly expressive.

Inquire with the winery

Vadio 2023 Rosé Bruto (Bairrada)

Offers citrus and light berry tones to go with silky bubbles and hints of toasted brioche and sea salt. Perfect as an aperitif.

title: Niche Italian Grape Varieties Are Trending in California
summary:
Golden State winemakers have been embracing lesser-known Italian grape varieties, and the results are absolutely magnifico.

The post Niche Italian Grape Varieties Are Trending in California appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
“I was on a quest to find the most non-Zinfandel thing out there,” said Evan Lewandowski as we tasted his 2024 Mahlon, made with 100% Arneis. The wine was lemony, a little salty, a little nutty, with a hint of almond blossom. It tasted like classic Arneis, the “little rascal” white grape of Italy’s Piedmont region. But we were not in Piedmont; we were at a table outside Evan’s winery, Ruth Lewandowski in Sonoma, drinking wine grown in Mendocino.

We moved on to his Obed Cuvée Zero, a blend of Riesling, Kerner, and Schiava that he calls “my Alto Adige blend.” These grapes—including the first commercial planting of Schiava and the second commercial planting of Kerner in California—also came from Mendocino, from Yorkville Highlands. Then there was his Feints bottling, a carbonic maceration of seven Piedmontese varieties, also grown in Mendocino: Dolcetto, Barbera, Nebbiolo, Friesa, Grignolino, Erbaluce, and Arneis. All three wines had very low, non-California alcohol levels under 13% abv.

“We’re having a lot of success in the vineyard with these Italian varieties,” Lewandowski told me. “They’re better positioned to survive in the current climate. These varieties have adapted to it.”

What’s happening at Ruth Lewandowski isn’t as unique as it sounds. On a recent visit to California, I spent a good deal of time tasting and talking about Italian varieties like Vermentino, Ribolla Gialla, Frappato, and Montepulciano. There’s an enthusiastic group of California growers experimenting with Italian grapes. While this movement is still relatively small—Chardonnay and Cabernet Sauvignon have nothing to worry about yet—many see these varieties as the way forward.

“All of this coincides with the overplanting of Cabernet in California,” said Chris Brockway, winemaker at Broc Cellars, which has been working with grapes like Nero d’Avola since 2013. “Italian varieties are popular right now. People seem to be less intimidated by them.”

Chris Walsh, winemaker at The End of Nowhere in Amador County, also works with Nero d’Avola and Arneis, along with Barbera. “In years past, Rhône varieties were popular,” Walsh said. “Now people are saying Italian varieties are what California should be growing.”

Lewandowski’s next-door neighbors, Ryme Cellars, started with Aglianico in 2007 and now work mostly with Italian grapes. “I remember one friend saying, ‘Are you sure you want to start with Italian varieties?’ People thought we were crazy for not going the traditional route,” Ryme’s winemaker Megan Glaab told me. “Now, there’s so much excitement for the Italian varieties, and growers are more excited to plant them.”

Beyond popularity and trends, there’s a straightforward, pressing reason for the new interest in Italian varieties in California. “The climate is changing, and you have to change with it,” Glaab said. “It’s too hot for Pinot on the valley floor of Russian River.” Italian varieties seem well suited to what Lewandowski calls “the 101 corridor” from Russian River to Mendocino.

“You come here in the summer and look around. We are not Bordeaux; we are not Burgundy. We are seeing the repercussions—we are harvesting Pinot Noir in August,” Lewandoski said.

During California’s extreme heat spell of 2022, for instance, Italian grapes survived very well. “These varieties can hang through that kind of heat. And you still have good natural acidity,” Glaab said.

More natural acidity and lower alcohol mean there’s less of a need to take a heavy hand in the winery. “With certain traditional grapes, you have to start manipulating them in the cellar. With the Italian varieties, you can be more non-interventionist,” Glaab said.

This isn’t the first time Italian varieties have gained popularity in California. There was the so-called “Cal-Ital” trend of the 1990s. “We think this is hip and cool now, but this has always been around,” said Dan Petroski, winemaker at Massican, which focuses on Italian white varieties like Friulano, Ribolla Gialla, Cortese, and Falanghina. “In California, there was more Barbera planted in the 1980s than Cabernet.”

It was none other than Mondavi who kicked off the Cal-Ital trend in the 1990s with their La Famiglia winery. But even that iconic producer’s magic touch couldn’t make Italian varieties happen. “Cal-Ital didn’t work,” Petroski said. “It’s more expensive to make wine in California than it is in Italy. Cal-Ital kind of faded. Pinot Grigio became Pinot Gris.”

One reason was that Sangiovese, the main Tuscan grape, never really worked in California. “A lot of people in California treated Sangiovese like Cabernet or Merlot. But if you do that, you lose the variety altogether,” Lewandoski told me.

Petroski points out that the iconic Tuscan estate Antinori planted several hundred acres of Sangiovese in Napa Valley in the 1990s. These days, Antinori only has a handful of acres left. “They realized over a 20-year period that Sangiovese was not a grape for the region,” Petroski said. “So Antinori got out of working with Italian grapes in California.”

This new movement in California tends to focus more on varieties from Piedmont, Friuli, and Sicily. Besides Arneis, Broc Cellars has had success with Friulian whites like Ribolla Gialla and Friulano, Sicilian reds like Nero d’Avola and Negroamaro, and a rosé from Montepulciano.

“One of the fun things about California right now is how open people are to different varieties,” said Brockway. “But we have to put some restraint on what we work with, and we don’t want to get too carried away. You want to be respectful of the grape. You have to realize you’re in a different location. Not everything does well here.”

One hurdle facing the rise of Italian varieties in California is that most winegrowers in the state are still not planting them. The number of vineyards with Italian varieties is still very small. As Petroski jokes about the winemakers working with Italian grapes: “If you put all of us in a room, we barely make 100,000 cases of wine.”

In fact, most of the winemakers working with Italian varieties still source from the same handful of vineyards. Perhaps most noteworthy is Fox Hill Vineyard, which has 60 acres on the Talmadge Bench in Mendocino, planted with two dozen Italian grape varieties. “It’s almost like a library or catalog of what Italian varieties can grow here,” says Brockway.

Fox Hill was planted in the 1980s and ’90s by Lowell and Barbara Stone, who lived on the property for 50 years and loved all things Italian. Originally, the vineyard was planted with Riesling and Chardonnay, but the Stones ripped those out and planted Ribolla Gialla, Aglianico, Nero d’Avola, Erbaluce, Vermentino, Grignolino, Freisa, Arneis, Sangiovese, Frappato, Dolcetto, Montepulciano, and Barbera, among others. “Some of those were suitcase cuttings,” Brockway said. Fox Hill’s Cortese, for instance, is said to have been smuggled in a suitcase from Gavi in 1985.

In 2014, Stone turned over much of the farming to Lewandowski and Sam Bilbro at Idlewild, while Broc Cellars and Ryme both bought grapes. In 2023, however, Fox Hill was acquired by Broc Cellars, which now runs the vineyard, which was certified organic in 2024.

California winemakers who work with Italian grapes credit Broc Cellars’ acquisition of Fox Hill as an essential turning point in preserving the fledgling movement. “If some multinational company had bought this vineyard, they would have torn everything out,” Lewandowski said. Other important vineyards for Italian grapes are Las Cimas in Russian River and Nichelini Ranch in Napa Valley.

One of the biggest challenges, several winemakers told me, is encouraging more California growers to plant more Italian varieties. “So many of our growers are like, ‘What should we plant?’” Lewandowski said. “I would always advocate for Italian varieties.”

Glaab would agree. “I can’t make enough Vermentino,” she told me. “It’s not going to take over Chardonnay or Sauvignon Blanc. But maybe it should.”

title: ‘Tupperwine Parties’ Bring the Tasting Room to Your Living Room
summary:
In-home tastings are becoming immensely popular—and a significant source of income—for wineries across California.

The post ‘Tupperwine Parties’ Bring the Tasting Room to Your Living Room appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Key Points

  • California wineries are bringing tasting room experiences directly into customer homes to combat falling tourism and rising travel expenses.
  • Winery representatives host informal, interactive gatherings where guests can taste wines and place orders for delivery.
  • These intimate “Tupperwine parties” foster personal connections, create approachable environment for guests, and boost long-term direct sales for wineries.

At first glance, it didn’t look much different than the usual backyard gathering at the Kettmanns: a dozen or so friends, eating tasty finger foods and sipping steady pours of fine wine while engaged in lively conservations as the sun set over Santa Barbara. 

But there were two new friends in the mix—Sara Fowler and Abby Graham, the winemaker and events manager, respectively, for Peju Winery in the Napa Valley. Toting stacks of marketing materials and a video player, the pair had come down from Rutherford (six hours away by car) to show us their version of an “in-home tasting,” in which wineries bring their tasting room into your house. 

Also called “Tupperwine parties,” this come-to-you format is becoming immensely popular—and a significant source of income—for wineries across California in this era of struggling wine sales and declining wine country visitation. These gatherings have become particularly prevalent in Napa and Paso Robles, with many wineries visiting customer homes as far away as Georgia and Connecticut as often as once or twice a month. 

Some, like Peju, advertise the service on their website, while others target prominent wine club members in specific markets. Most integrate these private tastings as add-on events when they are already visiting a region for larger consumer or trade tastings. 

“Visitation is down in the Napa Valley and most wine regions,” said Peju’s Nadia Kinkade, who oversees direct-to-consumer sales. “With the expense of travel and the difficulty of getting to the Napa Valley, it’s so much easier to get out on the road and come to them.”

It’s a big growth area for Alta Colina in Paso Robles, whose proprietor Maggie Tillman coined the term “Tupperwine parties.” It’s become a larger part of her sales strategy over the past two years, with visits to Phoenix, Chicago, Portland, Denver, and throughout California. “You throw a party, and we bring the wine,” said Tillman. “This is a more natural state to be enjoying wine.” 

Also in Paso Robles, Arnaud Fabre, who co-owns Benom Wines, started these tastings about three years ago, but has really ramped them up in the last year, with visits to Kansas City, St. Louis, Boston, and New Canaan in June alone. He recognizes that traveling to wine country might cost $5,000 for a weekend now. “If you take into consideration the food, the hotel, the visits, it adds up quite a bit,” said Fabre, and that leaves less budget to buy wine. 

During his tastings, he walks a line between party and seminar. “I want to be right in the middle,” he said. “It becomes a very interactive tasting where pretty much all the people attending ask so many questions. They all know each other so they don’t feel intimidated. It creates a very cool vibe.”

A New Way to Reach Wine Lovers

Versions of these tastings have been going on for many years—I went to one in Santa Barbara back in 2018—but they really ramped up as wineries scrambled to reach customers during the pandemic. That’s when Georgia Taylor started to experiment with the idea working for Thomas Rivers Brown at Post Parade Wines, particularly visiting Southern states where the social gathering rules weren’t so strict. 

“People were still anxious about coming up to Napa,” said Taylor. “It was a great opportunity to get out there and share our wine.”

In 2025, she was hired to bolster that same sort of outreach for Blackbird Vineyards, and now organizes in-home tastings monthly, often in cities where she is already traveling for larger consumer or industry events. “The cost of travel is so high, you really have to maximize your time in an area,” said Taylor. 

While some wineries set sales expectations for these tastings, Taylor thinks the amount of wine sold is besides the point. “There’s an intangible ROI on these,” she said. “I don’t think I have ever really seen an unsuccessful tasting.”

The experience creates an intimate bond. “We go into their home. We see what their kitchen looks like. We meet their family and their friends and the people who are important to them. We become an extension of that,” said Taylor. “It’s really hard to put a dollar amount on that.”

Given the country’s strict liquor laws—which change with every state—there are numerous legal considerations to keep in mind. The most basic one is that no wine can change hands on-site, and the transaction must occur via a bonded facility, although completing orders online makes that part easy. Said Tillman from Alta Colina, “I could take a Square payment on the moon, but I can’t hand you your wine.”

Returning to ‘What Napa Was All About’

Red tape aside, Taylor sees the in-home tasting as a return to the roots of it all. “It’s bringing it back to what Napa was all about,” she said. “It’s not like going to church. It doesn’t have to be formal and stuffy. You are there to interact and ask questions that you might be embarrassed to ask at a posh tasting.” 

When Tillman approached club member Bill Hughes in Phoenix to see if he’d like to host one of her Tupperwine parties, he agreed immediately. He invited 30 people, bought empanadas, and whipped up a pork tenderloin-in-barbecue sauce dish that went so well with the winery’s Mourvedre blend that he said it “synced people into a purchasing frenzy.” 

A few attendees signed up for the club themselves, and other friends have since visited the Paso Robles tasting room. “Once people get exposed to something like this, you can make believers out of them,” said Hughes. “People are asking us when we’re gonna do it again. I’m sure we will.”

My friends agreed it was a fun way to spend a Thursday evening, providing a little more education to an otherwise familiar affair. 

“The business model is a great idea from the customer perspective, especially for those people looking for a creative idea for hosting a gathering,” said my friend David Zell. Or as my neighbor Mackenzie Wildman summed it up: “I love a structured hang.”

title: Winemakers on This Tiny Volcanic Island Are Holding on for Dear Life
summary:
La Palma winemakers struggle against forces of nature—from wildfires to rabbits—to keep centuries-old traditions alive.

The post Winemakers on This Tiny Volcanic Island Are Holding on for Dear Life appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
In 2023, an inferno raged across La Palma, in Spain’s Canary Islands, engulfing ancient terraced vineyards near the Taburiente volcano crater. Years of drought had dried even the perpetual cloud forest to tinder.

The heat was sucked into the Vinos Tendal winery, causing an explosion that instantly destroyed everything. Metal turned to liquid, barrels combusted, glass melted. Miraculously, a stash of full bottles was spared. They were imprinted by the flash of heat, but still drinkable—nearly the only thing left to show for 30 years of work. Owners Nancy Castro Rodríguez and Constancio Ballesteros Magán were safe. Many of their vines perished, wiping out a library of La Palma grape varieties.

Vinos Tendal, one of La Palma’s largest wineries, partners with 40 of the approximately 900 growers on the island. Days away from harvest, the community scrambled and donated a new press, containers, and other equipment. The remaining grapes were picked by sheer force of will.

Like a phoenix from the ashes, their new winery opened this year in the same place. A gorgeous glass facade reflects the hillside, and its sheet-metal panels have oxidized to an iron red, like the surrounding soil. The wines haven’t missed a beat—think Jura meets volcano. Pure joy.

The Constant Unraveling

La Palma’s wine industry peaked in the early 1700s. Since then, it’s been a slow-motion tragedy playing out over the centuries. Praised by Shakespeare, imbibed by kings, and drunk from Caracas to Calcutta, wine was the island’s economic engine.

While banana plants have since taken over most of the vineyard land, the wine’s stature remains. Today, a mere 19 winemakers—up from three in 1993—are eking out a commercial existence. Of the 1,000-ish hectares under vine, less than 500 are part of La Palma DO. Growers are aging out, and with a dearth of eager youth to succeed them, there is a palpable fear that their specialized knowledge will disappear.

The wine is mostly slaked by the local market, at extremely low prices, inhibiting reinvestment and expansion even more. Re-establishing the wines into export markets would require a neatly digestible narrative, which, for La Palma, is a near impossibility.

An island smaller than New York City should tell a simple viticultural story. Yet wine growing here, 276 miles from the coast of Saharan Africa, is only possible due to precarious climatic conditions and diverse geological formations that create various microclimates. With localized viticulture, 23 grape varieties, and many styles, La Palma defies easy categorization.

Vines landed in the Canary Islands from all over Europe. While phylloxera decimated vineyards across the continent, the archipelago’s volcanic soils proved inhospitable to the louse, leaving its vines unharmed.

“It’s a snapshot of what viticulture was back in the 1500s,” says Vinicius Rodrigues, Spain, Portugal, and South America portfolio manager at importer Bowler Wine in New York. “The best way to explain all these indigenous varieties is Jurassic Park. These grapes were brought in, people left, and we lost track of where they came from. Then you come back years later, and it’s this carnival of completely different new things that mutated and have their own life now. Some bear resemblance to what we know from the continent; others are completely unknown.”

Explosions All Around

The bottom half of La Palma is formed by the jagged Cumbre Vieja and Cumbre Nueva mountains; the former is one of the most active on the planet. Halfway down its western side are the black, bilious remnants of a three-month-long eruption in 2021. Lava and noxious fumes destroyed buildings and vineyards, piling some under four feet of ash. It’s a miracle no one died.

A few more miles down the road lies Victoria Torres Pecis winery and its Las Machuqueras vineyard, 850 feet above the churning Atlantic. This 150-year-old field blend of mostly Listan Blanco and Malvasia is horizontally trained with cordons resting on little stakes a foot above the black ash, known locally as picón. Up to 12 feet below the picón is the fertile soil where an eruption blanketed a vineyard in 1721.

Adjacent to her parcel are hundreds of hand-stacked lava-rock walls, snaking across the landscape in precise formation. Vines hug the backside of the walls, buffeted from the constant wind, with hints of spring-green shoots peeking over their tops.

Victoria Torres Pecis is the fifth-generation owner of the vineyard; she calls it her ”patrimony.” Her father, Juan Matías, was considered the best vigneron on La Palma and the first breakout star in export markets in centuries. Torres Pecis’ wines have an almost mystical, timeless quality about them—stripped down, graceful, vibrating with the energy of the heartachingly beautiful, tremendously complicated place they are grown.

As the only producer with an established international audience, she is acutely aware of her position as the island’s wine ambassador. The existential pressure bears down on her otherwise joyous countenance, and comes out in a sort of melancholic panic, mixed with grief—for her father, the disappearing wisdom of her aging neighbors, abandoned vineyards, and the fact that she and her comrades are in a constant conflict with nature.

Cue the Rabbits

Torres Pecis’ current crusade? Rabbits. These little vegetarians might not be as bloodthirsty as the Rabbit of Caerbannog from Monty Python and the Holy Grail, but they are hungry. Islands are delicate ecosystems, and rabbits lived in symbiosis with La Palma’s vineyards for centuries, but now the rabbits are winning. Theoretically, hunters could help, but they have only exacerbated the problem by breeding rabbits so there are more around to hunt. Fencing, as Torres Pecis has installed, is expensive, ineffective, and mars the beautiful landscape.

She’s spent 10 years convincing authorities that what’s at stake is a national treasure. In April, the government committed to intervene, but bureaucracy moves slowly, and rabbits famously breed fast. In the meantime, she’s taking drastic measures to save her vineyard. She excavates up to 13 feet of ash to hit the soil below, adds compost, and, in a circus-strongman feat, rotates an entire vine 180 degrees down in the pit, then covers it up, leaving nothing but the end of a cane poking out of the surface. If she’s lucky, the cane will use the vine’s final reserves to create an almost new plant that will be protected from the rabbits.

Growers here are lucky to live without phylloxera. With 90% of their vines between 40 and 100 years old, they maintain a living connection to historic, heroic winemaking. This depth is reflected in refined wines that taste like nowhere else on earth.

Even more so, love is imbued in each bottle by a score of vignerons—including Castro Rodríguez and Torres Pecis, plus Onésima Pérez Rodríguez, the island’s first woman winemaker, and now Patricia Perdomo, one of its youngest.

To experience the wines, the place, and the people is to find yourself invested in its survival. Will there be enough time to build momentum and change the tides of fortune? Or is this fragile industry one eruption or climate catastrophe away from collapse? As Torres Pecis says, “La Palma is a place of contradiction.”
